title: Transactions, row locks, optimistic locking
idea: The consistency toolkit stops two writers corrupting shared rows: transactions group writes, row locks queue writers, and version checks reject stale writes.

analogy.text: One shared whiteboard. A lock is holding the only marker until you finish. A version check is writing only if the board still matches your photo of it.
analogy.breaks: Database locks release by themselves at COMMIT or ROLLBACK.

points: A transaction makes several writes succeed together or not at all.
`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` locks the row; other lockers wait until COMMIT.
Optimistic locking adds a version column; a stale write updates zero rows.
Use locks for hot rows, versions for rare conflicts, constraints wherever possible.

hero.title: FOR UPDATE queues the second writer

messages.label: BEGIN; SELECT FOR UPDATE
messages.note: A locks the SL-2 row and reads how many places are left.

messages.label: places_left = 2
messages.note: A now holds the row lock until it commits or rolls back.

messages.label: BEGIN; SELECT FOR UPDATE
messages.note: B asks for the same row and blocks. It reads nothing yet.

messages.label: UPDATE to 1; COMMIT
messages.note: A writes its decrement and commits. The lock is released.

messages.label: places_left = 1
messages.note: B wakes and reads the committed value, not the stale one.

messages.label: UPDATE to 0; COMMIT
messages.note: B's decrement builds on A's, so no booking is lost.

code.title: Lost update and two fixes
code.caption: Two clients on a real PostgreSQL. First the bug, then pessimistic locking, then optimistic locking.

walk.text: Three slots with two places each; a CHECK stops the count going negative.
No protection: both clients read, then both write. The second write erases the first.
Pessimistic: lock the row, check places, write, commit, all in one transaction.
Three bookings race for two places; print sorted results, never who won.
Optimistic: the UPDATE matches only if the version is still the one read.
A and B read the same version. A wins; B conflicts, re-reads and retries.

pitfalls: Never read, compute in code, then write back without a lock or version check.
Lock several rows in a fixed order, such as by id, to avoid deadlocks.
Keep locking transactions short; never call a payment provider while holding locks.

quiz.q: What does the B writes v1 line print?
quiz.why: A's update raised the version to 2. B's UPDATE requires version = 1, matches zero rows, so `rowCount` is 0 and it returns CONFLICT.

takeaway: Group with transactions, queue with row locks, detect with versions.
